bib.title: Mo' Models, Mo' Problems: How to best select model pools when designing Multi-Agent Systems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Mo' Models, Mo' Problems: How to best select model pools when designing Multi-Agent Systems", Marjanovic, Xu, Laptev, Nalbandyan, Arakelyan, Bakhaturina (Copenhagen, NVIDIA). arXiv:2609.17306v1 [cs.MA], 15 Sep 2026. Preprint (formatted as an ACL-style paper; no venue stated). Code repo linked in abstract.
COVERAGE: 72036 of 72036 chars read (main text, limitations, references skimmed, appendices A.1-A.7, B.1-B.2, subset tables). Figure bodies (plots) not read; figures 4/5 numbers are not in the text. Many HLE/FS/GPQA accuracy tables live only in figures, so I cannot quote them.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Growing a heterogeneous model pool nearly always lowers achieved MAS performance, even though oracle potential rises.
 number: none given as a single figure (the gains are plotted, not tabulated in text)
 setup: 23 models (2B-1.6T, 6 families, 2024-2026), 5 generations per model per question; pool sizes k in {3,5,10,15,20}; routing, majority vote, LLM-judge (GenSelect, gpt-oss-120b); HLE, GPQA-Diamond, FrontierScience-Olympiad; no tools or retrieval. Gain is measured against the best single model inside each pool.
 quote: "For actual MAS performance in Figure 5, one pattern is clear: more models nearly always decreases performance. Most intentional groupings give performance lower than the baseline best model, and often lower than a random set of models."
 where: Sec 4.3, p.5

2. Only same-family pools occasionally beat the best single model; the family result is the least-bad rather than a large gain.
 number: small: "+2% on FS, +<1% on GPQA" (Gemma4 family, accuracy-optimised groupings)
 setup: Family pools (Olmo, Llama, Qwen3, Qwen3.5, Gemma, gpt-oss) include all family members, so k is limited. Best is Gemma4; OLMo3 and Qwen3 are highly variable. On HLE only single-family MAS beat the baseline.
 quote: "in addition to improved performance on HLE with Gemma4 family architeture, we find a small MAS gain (+2% on FS, +<1% on GPQA) with Accuracy and Accuracy-optimised metrics"
 where: Sec 4.3, p.5. Also "in most cases, this means the least detriment to performance rather than a large improvement."

3. Homogeneous repetition at matched model does help: majority and judge over the best single model beat a single sample, while heterogeneous pools fall below that.
 number: 29.4% pass@1 -> 32.2% majority@5 -> 36.5% judge@5
 setup: HLE, best single model (Best(m)), 5 samples of the same model; judge is gpt-oss-120b GenSelect. Note that compute is NOT matched across rows (5x samples vs 1x). The paper does not run a compute-matched comparison.
 quote: "Despite an increase in the best single-agent systems using majority vote (29.4% pass@1Best(m) to 32.2% majority@5 Best(m) on HLE), nearly all heterogeneous MAS groups decline in performance"; "judge@5 Best(m) = 36.5% on HLE"
 where: Sec 4.3, p.5

4. Oracle (pass@k-style upper bound) is a poor predictor of achieved gain; selecting for diversity predicts least and sometimes delivers most.
 number: none
 setup: Oracle = best pass@1 achievable by any model in the pool. Accuracy-ranked and LLM-chosen pools have the highest oracle; IoU/Error-diverse pools the lowest. In routing, IoU-diverse pools did best, and only IoU and Family gave positive routing gains. Under majority vote, error/IoU-diverse pools collapsed.
 quote: "Groupings with limited prophesized improvements (as measured via oracle performance, such as shared model families or correct answer diversity), often show the best actual performance across MAS architecture."
 where: Conclusion, p.6; Sec 4.2-4.3

5. Model pairs are more alike in what they get right than in their errors, and specialist models do not add distinct expertise.
 number: rM = 0.931 (correct-answer similarity), rM = 0.384 (error similarity); size vs accuracy rs = 0.583
 setup: 15.5k-question calibration set; Mantel tests on pairwise distance matrices. Deepseek-v4 and Qwen3.5 make very similar errors (>0.8 similarity, App A.5). Llama-3.1-8B generalist beat its physics/chemistry-tuned derivatives on all domains, including physics and chemistry.
 quote: "More accurate models get similar questions correct (rM = 0.931, p < .01), yet their errors are only mildly correlated (rM = 0.384, p < .01)."
 where: Fig 2 caption, p.4; Sec 4.1

6. Homogeneous MAS improve with complexity while heterogeneous ones degrade; the authors read this as a need for architectures built for heterogeneous pools.
 number: none
 quote: "our baseline homogeneous MAS systems performance increased with MAS complexity, suggesting that these architectures may be best suited for homogeneous systems"
 where: Conclusion, p.6

LIMITS
- Authors concede: only three simple MAS (one routing backbone, AvengersPro-style clustering; embedding-cluster majority vote, cosine threshold 0.15; one stratified GenSelect judge). They suggest judge context length at high k may cause part of the judge's poor result. They also note no tool use or retrieval, only scientific reasoning (no math or code), and a single judge model (gpt-oss-120b).
- The judge is more lenient than a human: on a 100-answer HLE subsample, agreement is 93%, Cohen's kappa 0.63, so accuracies are probably inflated.
- Family pools cannot reach every k. No debate or interaction-based (during-generation) MAS. They state that heterogeneous MAS is not futile and that other studies report gains.
- Not shown: any compute-matched comparison (cost per query is not equated across single, k-model, and 5-sample systems); self-consistency vs self-refine; confidence intervals or seeds are not mentioned in the text. Gains are mostly in plots, so exact per-condition numbers are unavailable here. Model list is dated to 2024-2026 releases.
- Caution for the chapter: the finding is about which models are in a mixed pool, not about number of agents of one model. Do not cite it as evidence that more same-model samples fail; item 3 suggests the opposite.

BUILDS ON
Ensembles: Dietterich 2000; Breiman 1996 (bagging), 2001; Wolpert 1992 (stacking); Jacobs et al. 1991 (mixture of experts). Majority vote: Wang et al. 2023 (self-consistency); Li et al. 2024 (more agents). Judge: Toshniwal et al. 2025 (GenSelect). Routing: AvengersPro (Zhang et al. 2025), FrugalFoE (Wang et al. 2024a), Tryage (Hari and Thomson 2023). Multiagent debate: Du et al. 2024 (ICML). Heterogeneous ensembles: LLM-Blender (Jiang et al. 2023, ACL), DeePEn (Huang et al. 2024, NeurIPS). Diversity: Abdulaal et al. 2025 (ICLR), Yang et al. 2026 (more diversity helps, contradicted here for pool size), Kim et al. 2026b. Benchmarks: HLE (Phan et al. 2026, Nature), GPQA (Rein et al. 2024), FrontierScience (Wang et al. 2026).

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- Figure 5 (p.5): "Actual gains of each MAS subset and architecture with increasing k. With larger candidate pools, we see larger losses in performance (compared to the single best model of the set). On HLE, Only MAS with models from one model family show improvements over the baseline best model." Best candidate: shows the loss with k for all three architectures. Pair with Figure 4 (oracle rising with k) for the oracle-vs-achieved gap.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction clean for text; icons/markers (symbols for selection strategies) are lost in extraction, so some strategy labels in Sec 4.3 are ambiguous (for example which symbol is Accuracy vs Error). Figures are images and were not extracted. The paper is dated Sept 2026 and cites 2026 models; "Kimi-K2.5 Agent Swarm" is cited as Lumen AI 2026 as printed.
